subject: ux-ui-design
name: UX/UI Design
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance).

units.title: Introduction to UX and UI
topics: What is UX? What is UI?
Seeing the ideas: interface types, the honeycomb, contrast, the UX loop and a good form

sections.title: What is UX? What is UI?
Seeing the ideas: interface types, the honeycomb, contrast, the UX loop and a good form

summary: UX is the entire experience; UI is its visible and tangible layer. UX designers work on research, flows and structure; UI designers on visual and component design.
The three guiding principles are usability, accessibility and simplicity, supported by consistency, feedback, affordance and error prevention.
UX has six disciplines that feed each other in a loop.
Interfaces range from CLI to GUI, menu-driven, voice and conversational; the right type depends on users and context.
Good designs are useful, usable, findable, credible, accessible, desirable and valuable.
Figma, Adobe XD and Sketch are the standard design tools.

units.title: User Interaction Design and UX Research
topics: Seeing the ideas: the process, mind map, sample sizes, persona, journey map and Crazy 8s

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: the process, mind map, sample sizes, persona, journey map and Crazy 8s

summary: UX design is an iterative loop; user-centred design involves users at every stage.
A mind map explores a problem; research methods (interviews, surveys, competitive analysis) provide evidence, qualitative and quantitative.
Personas and journey maps turn research into shared, human, visual artefacts; opportunities appear at the pain points.
Ideation produces many options using mood boards, brainstorming and sketching before anything is built.

units.title: User Interface Design
topics: Human considerations in interface and screen design
Seeing the ideas: interaction styles, Fitts and Hick, touch targets, the process, breakpoints and response time

sections.title: Human considerations in interface and screen design
Seeing the ideas: interaction styles, Fitts and Hick, touch targets, the process, breakpoints and response time

summary: GUIs use windows, icons, menus and a pointer; web UIs add browser conventions, unknown screens and scanning behaviour.
Five interaction styles each fit a task and user: command line, menus, forms, direct manipulation, anthropomorphic.
UI principles stress consistency, feedback, affordance, error prevention and control; Fitts's and Hick's laws quantify pointing and choosing.
The UI process runs from understanding and structure through wireframes, visual design, prototype, test and hand-off.
Design must respect human limits (perception, memory, attention, motor skill, culture) and technical limits (devices, platforms, performance, network, accessibility technology).

units.title: UI Components
topics: Seeing the ideas: menus, windows, controls, icons and images

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: menus, windows, controls, icons and images

summary: Menus let users recognise commands; format them consistently, keep them short and well grouped, and pick the type — bar, pull-down, cascading, pop-up, tear-off, iconic — by the task.
Windows may be tiled, overlapping or cascading; primary, secondary windows and dialog boxes serve different roles; modal dialogs should be rare.
Controls are operable, text-entry, selection or other; choosing the proper control for the task prevents errors and speeds use.
Icons and images must be meaningful, consistent, accessible and technically optimised.

units.title: UI Design Considerations
topics: Seeing the ideas: grids, Gestalt, colour, type, hierarchy and navigation

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: grids, Gestalt, colour, type, hierarchy and navigation

summary: Layout uses grids, reading patterns, Gestalt principles and white space to make structure visible.
Colour schemes are built from a primary, secondary, neutral and semantic palette; contrast must meet WCAG ratios and colour must never be the sole signal.
Typography chooses one or two legible families, readable sizes, line height, line length and a consistent type scale; Devanagari needs extra leading.
Responsive design combines fluid grids, flexible media and media queries, designed mobile-first.
Visual hierarchy ranks elements through alignment, colour, contrast, proximity, size, texture and time.
Navigation comes in global, local, utility, associative and inline forms and follows a model — hub-and-spoke, fully connected, tree, stepwise, pyramid or flat — chosen to fit the content.

units.title: Wireframing and Prototyping
topics: From idea to product: the fidelity ladder
Creating a simple clickable prototype (the lab method)
Seeing the ideas: sketches, wireframes, prototypes, storyboards and motion

sections.title: From idea to product: the fidelity ladder
Creating a simple clickable prototype (the lab method)
Seeing the ideas: sketches, wireframes, prototypes, storyboards and motion

summary: Wireframes show structure and priority without style; mock-ups add the visual design; prototypes make them interactive so they can be tested.
Low-fidelity prototypes (paper, grey boxes) test concepts early and cheaply; high-fidelity ones test visuals and detailed interaction late.
Prototyping tools such as Figma link frames with triggers, actions and transitions; software prototypes may be throwaway or evolutionary.
Storyboards tell the user's story in context and reveal needs that screens alone hide.
Animation should orient, give feedback and focus attention, with sensible duration and easing and respect for accessibility.

units.title: Design Evaluation
topics: Evaluation through expert analysis and user participation
Seeing the ideas: tests, numbers, heuristics and task models

sections.title: Evaluation through expert analysis and user participation
Seeing the ideas: tests, numbers, heuristics and task models

summary: Evaluate iteratively: formative evaluation improves a design while it is made, summative evaluation judges the result.
Usability tests observe representative users on realistic tasks; moderated tests give depth, unmoderated tests give scale; five users per round find most problems.
Analyse with success rate, time, errors, SUS and severity-rated findings, then recommend fixes by priority.
Expert methods (heuristic evaluation, walkthroughs) and user methods complement each other; paradigms range from quick-and-dirty to field studies and predictive models.
DECIDE structures an evaluation plan; Nielsen's ten heuristics structure an expert review.
Task analysis (HTA) and KLM predict and compare task effort.

units.title: Advanced Techniques: VUI and NLP-based UI
topics: Command and control versus conversational UI
Personas, avatars, actors and video games
Seeing the ideas: voices, speech, dialogs, characters and wearables

sections.title: Command and control versus conversational UI
Personas, avatars, actors and video games
Seeing the ideas: voices, speech, dialogs, characters and wearables

summary: VUI and NLP-based UIs give hands-free and natural interaction but hide their options and suffer from recognition and ambiguity errors.
Command-and-control uses fixed commands and is reliable; conversational UIs use intents, slots and context and are flexible but less predictable.
A designed persona gives a voice or chatbot a consistent personality; avatars and game-style characters can engage users when their realism matches their ability.
Speech recognition converts speech to text through acoustic and language models; Nepali is a low-resource language with higher error rates.
Dialog management tracks state, chooses the next action, confirms risk, and repairs errors with a human fallback.
Wearables demand glanceable, minimal, context-aware, haptic-rich design.
